newsitem.title: AZERBAIJAN: Azeri leader cancels trip after Armenian PM named.
newsitem.headline: Azeri leader cancels trip after Armenian PM named.

text.p: President Haydar Aliyev cancelled a planned trip to Pakistan on Friday, a day after the leader of Azerbaijan's breakaway Nagorno-Karabakh region became the prime minister in neighbouring Armenia.
But overall Azerbaijan reacted cautiously to the appointment of the Karabakh leader, Robert Kocharyan, which some Western diplomats predict could set back regional peace efforts.

Aliyev's press service said parliamentary speaker Murtuz Aleskerov would replace the president at the summit meeting of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference (OIC) in Islamabad due to be held on Sunday.

Political analysts have suggested that the cancellation was linked to Armenian President Levon Ter-Petrosyan's surprise decision on Thursday. But no official reason was given for Aliyev's change of plans and Azeri officials kept low profile.
"I am going to reserve comment until I can determine the motive for (Ter-Petrosyan's) act," Azeri Foreign Minister Hasan Hasanov told reporters by telephone in the Azeri capital Baku.

Deputy Foreign Minister Araz Azimov took a more criticial line, saying Armenia "wanted to reinforce its annexation of the territory of Azerbaijan", but his comments appeared to be a personal rather than an official reaction.
Only Ittibar Mamedov, leader of the opposition National Independence Party, slammed Kocharyan's appointment.
"This...shows again that the so-called Nagorno-Karabakh republic is a puppet regime...that this region has been annexed by Armenia," Mamedov told Azerbaijan's Turan news agency.

Azeri government offices were closed on Thursday and Friday for the Navruz holiday, a spring rite of pagan origin celebrated in many Moslem countries. Newspapers did not appear on Friday and state radio and television made no mention of the news.

Surrounded by Azeri territory, Karabakh is populated mostly by ethnic Armenians. It broke away from Baku's rule in the late 1980s, triggering years of fighting between Moslem Azeris and Christian Armenians in which thousands were killed.

Western diplomats in Baku close to negotiations between Azerbaijan and Armenia over Karabakh's future said Kocharyan's appointment seemed to indicate that Yerevan had decided to take a harder line on the issue.
"I think that this was a surprise for the Azeri government and that it might influence peace negotiations very negatively. It will be much harder to make progress," said one diplomat.
He said he thought Ter-Petrosyan, who gave no explanation for his decision, had acted to pacify nationalist and opposition groups who have until now seen his rule as illegitimate.

The 51-year old leader sent tanks into the streets of the capital Yerevan last year to put down protests by opponents who accused him of rigging presidential elections. Foreign monitors said the vote was marred by fraud and irregularities.
"Ter-Petrosyan's domestic position has been considerably weakened. He is under great pressure to find common ground with the opposition," said the diplomat.

On Friday Russia's Interfax news agency quoted Armenian officials in Yerevan as saying the appointment of Kocharyan would not have a negative effect on peace talks, provided Azerbaijan did not try to exploit the move for its own benefit.
